source_refs.note: Chapter 7 exercise (PDF 170-173, printed 167-170): MCQs keyed from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to the written questions, numericals worked step by step and checked against the printed answers; corrections in the lesson.

blocks.prompt: 7.1 The simple wave speed equation is represented by:
blocks.explanation: A crest moves one wavelength λ in one period T, so v = λ/T = fλ (Eq. 7.1). The other options are the speed of a body, linear speed in circular motion and average velocity.

blocks.prompt: 7.2 The principle of superposition in waves is stated as:

options.text: the displacement of a wave is the sum of the displacements of its individual components
the velocity of a wave is the product of its individual components
the frequency of a wave is the difference of its individual components
the amplitude of a wave is the ratio of its individual components

blocks.explanation: When two or more waves act on a particle together, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂ + … + yₙ (7.2).

blocks.prompt: 7.3 A node in a stationary wave is:
blocks.explanation: At a node the resultant displacement is always zero; nodes are λ/2 apart (7.4).

blocks.prompt: 7.4 An antinode in a stationary wave is:
blocks.explanation: Antinodes vibrate with the largest amplitude (the sum of the two component amplitudes); they lie midway between nodes (7.4).

blocks.prompt: 7.5 Stationary waves are defined as:

options.text: waves that move with a constant velocity
waves that move with a changing velocity
waves that oscillate in a fixed position
waves that propagate through a medium

blocks.explanation: Stationary (standing) waves oscillate in a fixed position without moving forward; nodes and antinodes stay at fixed places (7.4).

blocks.prompt: 7.6 Harmonics are:

options.text: integer multiples of a fundamental frequency
integer submultiples of a fundamental frequency
non-integer multiples of a fundamental frequency

blocks.explanation: Harmonics are the frequencies f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, …, nf₁, i.e. fₙ = nf₁ with n = 1, 2, 3, … (7.5).

blocks.prompt: 7.7 The result of constructive interference between two waves is represented as:
blocks.explanation: In constructive interference crest meets crest (path difference nλ), so the displacements add and the resultant amplitude increases (7.3).

blocks.prompt: 7.8 If the amplitude of the wave is tripled, then the amount of energy is increased by:
blocks.explanation: Intensity (energy) ∝ A² (I = kA², Eq. 7.13). With 3A the energy becomes (3)² = 9 times.

blocks.prompt: 7.9 What type of waves do headphones use to produce sound?
blocks.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs a medium (air) to travel (7.1). The headphone's diaphragm vibrates the air next to the ear.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Options (b), (c) and (d) all describe sound: in air sound is a mechanical wave that travels as a longitudinal pressure wave. The chapter (7.1) classifies sound waves as mechanical waves, so (b) is the expected answer.

blocks.prompt: 7.10 The typical frequency range of microwaves is:
blocks.explanation: Microwaves have wavelengths of millimetres to centimetres (7.7). With f = c/λ: c/(30 cm) = 10⁹ Hz and c/(3 mm) = 10¹¹ Hz, so the range is about 10⁹ - 10¹¹ Hz. (The exponents are printed very small; they are read as 3-5, 5-7, 7-9 and 9-11.)

blocks.prompt: 7.11 The bending of waves around an obstacle is called as:
blocks.explanation: Diffraction is the bending of waves around sharp edges or corners of obstacles, or their spreading beyond a gap (7.8).

blocks.prompt: 7.12 The Doppler Effect used in astronomy is for:
blocks.explanation: Astronomers measure the red shift or blue shift of a star's or galaxy's spectral lines and from it calculate its speed (7.12).

blocks.prompt: 7.1 What are the conditions for interference to occur?
blocks.explanation:
1. The two sources must be coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference (e.g. two speakers driven by one audio generator).
2. The waves must overlap while travelling in the same direction.
3. Constructive interference where path difference ΔS = nλ; destructive where ΔS = (2n + 1)λ/2.

blocks.prompt: 7.2 Differentiate between constructive and destructive interference of waves.
blocks.explanation: In constructive interference the waves reinforce each other; in destructive interference they cancel each other.

rows: Crest meets crest (compression meets compression)
Crest meets trough (compression meets rarefaction)
Path difference ΔS = nλ, n = 0, ±1, ±2, …
Path difference ΔS = (2n + 1)λ/2
Resultant amplitude increases: y = y₁ + y₂
Resultant amplitude decreases: y = y₁ − y₂ (zero if y₁ = y₂)
Loud sound (bright light)
Faint or no sound (darkness)

blocks.prompt: 7.3 What are coherent waves and coherent sources? Give examples.
blocks.explanation:
Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference (usually in phase).
Coherent sources are sources that emit such waves.
Examples: two loudspeakers driven by the same audio generator (7.3); light from a laser; two slits lit by one monochromatic (sodium) lamp.

blocks.prompt: 7.4 Distinguish between longitudinal and transverse waves.
blocks.explanation: The difference is the direction in which the particles vibrate compared with the direction of travel of the wave.

rows: Particles vibrate along (parallel to) the direction of travel
Particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel
Made of compressions and rarefactions
Made of crests and troughs
Wavelength: distance between two consecutive compressions
Wavelength: distance between two consecutive crests
Example: sound waves in air
Example: waves on a string, light waves

blocks.prompt: 7.5 Is it possible for two identical waves travelling in the same direction along a string to give rise to a stationary wave? How is it so?
blocks.explanation:
No. A stationary wave is formed only when two identical waves (same frequency and amplitude) travel in opposite directions, e.g. an incident and a reflected wave (7.4).
Two identical waves moving in the same direction simply interfere and give a travelling wave of larger (or smaller) amplitude that still moves forward, so no fixed nodes and antinodes form.

blocks.prompt: 7.6 How would you apply Doppler effect in studying cardiac problems in humans?
blocks.explanation:
In Doppler echocardiography ultrasound is sent into the heart and blood vessels. It reflects from moving blood cells with a changed (Doppler-shifted) frequency.
From this shift the speed and direction of blood flow are found, which detects valve stenosis or regurgitation and blocked vessels, measures cardiac output and helps set pacemakers (7.12).

blocks.prompt: 7.7 What is meant by diffraction of waves? For what purpose, the ripple tank is used?
blocks.explanation:
Diffraction is the bending of waves around sharp edges of obstacles or their spreading through a gap comparable to the wavelength.
A ripple tank is used to generate water waves and to demonstrate wave properties: reflection, refraction and diffraction (e.g. how gap width affects diffraction).

blocks.prompt: 7.1 Which measurement of a wave is the most important when determining the wave's intensity?
blocks.explanation:
The amplitude.
The energy carried by a mechanical wave depends on the displacement (amplitude) of the particles, so intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude: I ∝ A², I = kA² (7.13).
So a small change in amplitude changes the intensity a lot: doubling A makes I four times, tripling A makes it nine times.
(Intensity itself is power per unit area, I = P/A, in W m⁻².)

blocks.prompt: 7.2 Can you apply Doppler effect to light waves? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. The Doppler effect applies to all waves, including electromagnetic (light) waves (7.12).
- A star or galaxy moving away from the Earth shows a red shift: its spectral lines move to longer wavelength.
- One moving towards the Earth shows a blue shift: shorter wavelength.
By comparing its spectrum with a laboratory source, astronomers measure the shift and calculate the speed, using f′ = [c/(c + uₛ)] f for a receding source (Example 7.12). The same idea is used in radar (aeroplanes), radar speed traps and satellite navigation.

blocks.prompt: 7.3 Can you compare the compressions and rarefactions of the longitudinal wave with the peaks and troughs of the transverse wave? Discuss.
blocks.explanation: Yes. A compression (particles crowded, high pressure) corresponds to a crest (peak), and a rarefaction (particles spread out, low pressure) corresponds to a trough. In both waves the distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive crests is one wavelength λ, and v = fλ holds. The difference is the direction of vibration.

rows: Compression: region of high density and pressure
Crest: point of maximum positive displacement
Rarefaction: region of low density and pressure
Trough: point of maximum negative displacement
Particles vibrate along the direction of travel
Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel
λ = distance between two consecutive compressions
λ = distance between two consecutive crests

blocks.prompt: 7.4 How should a source of sound move with respect to an observer so that the frequency of its sound does not change? Write two examples.
blocks.explanation:
The frequency does not change when there is no relative motion between source and observer along the line joining them, i.e. the distance between them stays constant.
Examples:
1. The source and observer move with the same velocity: passengers in a moving car or train hear its horn at its normal pitch (in Example 7.10, if both trucks had the same speed, uₛ = 0 and f′ = f).
2. The source moves in a circle around the observer at the centre: a whistle whirled round on a string is heard by the person holding it at a constant pitch.

blocks.prompt: 7.5 Why is it difficult to recognize beats when the frequency difference is greater than 10 Hz? Exemplify.
blocks.explanation:
Number of beats per second = difference of frequencies. If the difference is more than 10 Hz, more than 10 loud sounds come every second, i.e. one loud sound less than 1/10 s after the last. The ear keeps the impression of a sound for about 1/10 s (persistence of hearing, beyond the chapter), so it cannot separate the loud and faint sounds and hears one continuous (rough) note (7.9).
Example: forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz give 4 beats/s, clearly heard; forks of 256 Hz and 280 Hz would give 24 beats/s, which cannot be counted.

blocks.prompt: 7.1 State and explain the principle of superposition of waves. Apply this principle to elaborate the working of noise canceling headphones.
blocks.explanation:
Principle of superposition: If a particle of the medium is acted upon by two (or more) waves at the same time, its resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
y = y₁ + y₂ + … + yₙ, or y(x,t) = y₁(x,t) + y₂(x,t) + … + yₙ(x,t)
Explanation:
(i) Waves in phase (crest on crest): y = y₁ + y₂; if y₁ = y₂, y = 2y₁ (reinforcement).
(ii) Waves in opposite phase (crest on trough): y = y₁ + (−y₂) = y₁ − y₂; if y₁ = y₂, y = 0 (cancellation).
The principle applies to linear (small-amplitude) waves and leads to interference (same frequency, same direction), beats (slightly different frequencies, same direction) and stationary waves (same frequency, opposite directions).
Noise-cancelling headphones:
1. One or more microphones in the headphones pick up the ambient noise (chatter, engine rumble).
2. The signal goes to an amplifier and a processing unit.
3. The processor produces an anti-noise signal: the same amplitude as the noise but opposite in phase.
4. The anti-noise is played through the speakers together with the music or voice.
5. At the ear the noise (y₁) and anti-noise (−y₁) superpose: y = y₁ − y₁ = 0, so the noise is cancelled by destructive interference and only the wanted sound is heard.
Real headphones use complex algorithms and several microphones, but the basic principle is superposition.

blocks.prompt: 7.2 What are standing waves? Illustrate a detailed experiment that demonstrates the standing waves using stretched strings.
blocks.explanation:
Standing (stationary) waves: waves formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions. The pattern does not move forward; nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) stay at fixed positions. Distance between consecutive nodes = λ/2; node to next antinode = λ/4.
Experiment (stretched string):
Apparatus: a string of length l clamped at both ends and kept stretched with tension F; m = mass per unit length.
(a) Plucked at its middle: two transverse waves travel to the two ends, are reflected back and superpose, forming stationary waves. The clamped ends are nodes, with one antinode in the middle: the string vibrates in one loop.
l = λ₁/2, so λ₁ = 2l
Speed of waves on the string: v = √(F/m)
f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/2l = (1/2l)√(F/m) (fundamental frequency, first harmonic)
(b) Plucked at one quarter of its length (at an antinode position): the string vibrates in two loops.
l = λ₂/2 + λ₂/2, so λ₂ = l
f₂ = v/λ₂ = v/l = 2(v/2l) = 2f₁ (second harmonic)
(c) Vibrating in n loops ((n + 1) nodes, n antinodes):
λₙ = 2l/n, fₙ = n(v/2l) = nf₁, n = 1, 2, 3, …
Results:
1. Stationary waves on a string have only the discrete frequencies f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, … (harmonic series); this is the quantization of frequencies. Other frequencies are quickly damped.
2. As the number of loops increases, f increases and λ decreases, but fλ = v stays the same.
3. The frequency can be changed by changing the tension (tightening the pegs) or the length (moving the fingers), as in a guitar or violin.
(In the laboratory the string is often driven by an electric vibrator and kept taut over a pulley by hanging weights; changing the weights or length shows 1, 2, 3 … loops. This set-up is beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 7.3 Find the frequencies of the harmonics produced in organ pipe when it is open at one end and when it is open at both ends.
blocks.explanation:
In an organ pipe stationary longitudinal waves are set up in the air column. An open end is an antinode (air moves freely); a closed end is a node. Let the length be l and the speed of sound v.
Case 1: Pipe open at both ends (antinodes at both ends)
(a) Fundamental mode: one node in the middle.
l = λ₁/4 + λ₁/4 = λ₁/2, so λ₁ = 2l
f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/2l (fundamental frequency, first harmonic)
(b) Second mode: three antinodes, two nodes.
l = λ₂/4 + λ₂/2 + λ₂/4 = λ₂, so f₂ = v/l = 2f₁
(c) nth mode: fₙ = n(v/2l) = nf₁, λₙ = 2l/n, n = 1, 2, 3, …
So all harmonics f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, … are present.
Case 2: Pipe closed at one end (node at the closed end, antinode at the open end)
(a) Fundamental mode: one node, one antinode.
l = λ₁/4, so λ₁ = 4l
f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/4l
(b) Next mode: two nodes, two antinodes.
l = λ₃/4 + λ₃/2 = 3λ₃/4, so λ₃ = 4l/3
f₃ = v/λ₃ = 3v/4l = 3f₁ (third harmonic)
(c) nth mode: fₙ = n(v/4l) = nf₁, λₙ = 4l/n, n = 1, 3, 5, …
So only odd harmonics f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, … are present.
Conclusion: a pipe open at both ends is richer in harmonics; for the same length its fundamental (v/2l) is double that of a closed pipe (v/4l).

blocks.prompt: 7.4 Define and exemplify diffraction of waves. Describe this phenomenon by ripple tank experiment.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Diffraction is the bending of waves around the sharp edges or corners of obstacles, or the spreading of waves beyond a barrier. It occurs when the obstacle or opening (slit) is comparable in size to the wavelength. The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading.
It is shown by all kinds of waves: water, sound, light and other electromagnetic waves.
Examples:
1. We hear sound around corners or through a doorway, because sound waves bend around the corners.
2. X-rays are diffracted by crystals, since the spacing of the atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength.
3. White light is split into colours by a fine diffraction grating; the fine rulings of a compact disc act as a grating.
Ripple tank experiment:
Apparatus: a tank of water, a vibrator (a motorized oscillating needle or bar), obstacles (a small rectangular block or a semicircular barrier) used to make gaps of different widths.
Procedure:
1. The vibrator produces a series of plane (parallel) or circular water waves.
2. Two obstacles are placed in the path to leave a gap of a chosen width.
3. The pattern of the waves passing through the gap is observed; the experiment is repeated with different gap widths.
Observations:
- When the gap is small compared with the wavelength, diffraction is large: the waves bend around the edges and spread out in a semicircular pattern.
- When the gap is wide compared with the wavelength, diffraction is small: the waves pass straight through with little bending.
Conclusion: the amount of diffraction depends on the ratio of gap width to wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 7.5 What is meant by the term beats? Prove that number of beats per second is equal to the difference between the frequencies of vibrating tuning forks.
blocks.explanation:
Beats: When two sound waves of slightly different frequencies, travelling in the same direction, overlap, the loudness of the sound rises and falls periodically between maximum and minimum. These periodic variations are called beats.
Proof (book's example):
Let tuning fork A have fA = 32 Hz and fork B (loaded with wax) fB = 28 Hz, sounded together.
- At an instant X both waves have displacement in the same direction: the resultant is large and a loud sound is heard.
- In 1/8 s, A makes 4 vibrations and B makes 3.5, so A gains half a vibration: the displacements are opposite at Y, giving minimum (faint or no) sound.
- In another 1/8 s (1/4 s from X), A has gained one full vibration: the waves are again in step at Z and a loud sound is heard.
So one loud sound comes every 1/4 s, i.e. 4 beats per second, and fA − fB = 32 − 28 = 4 Hz.
General proof: Let T be the time between two successive loud sounds. In this time fork A makes one vibration more than fork B (it gets one full vibration ahead), so
fA T − fB T = 1
fA − fB = 1/T
The number of beats per second is f_beat = 1/T, therefore
f_beat = fA − fB
Hence the number of beats per second equals the difference between the frequencies of the two tuning forks.
(Beats are used to tune instruments: the string is adjusted until no beats are heard against a standard note. They are not recognized when the difference exceeds about 10 Hz.)

blocks.prompt: 7.6 What do you understand by progressive waves? Discuss the intensity of progressive waves.
blocks.explanation:
Progressive waves: A progressive (travelling) wave travels through a medium in a definite direction and transfers energy from one point to another, as opposed to a stationary wave. Examples: water waves, sound waves, light waves.
Intensity: the amount of energy transmitted per unit area per unit time in the direction of propagation of a progressive wave. It measures the power of the wave; symbol I, unit W m⁻².
I = E/(A × t) = (E/t)/A
I = P/A (since E/t = P, the power)
where E = energy (J), t = time (s), A = area (m²), P = power (W).
Dependence on amplitude: In mechanical waves energy is stored as kinetic and potential energy of the particles, and it depends on their displacement (amplitude) from the mean position. So
I ∝ A², or I = kA² (7.13)
where k is a constant depending on the wave and the medium. Doubling the amplitude makes the intensity four times.
Dependence on distance: For a point source radiating power P equally in all directions, the energy spreads over a sphere of area 4πr², so I = P/(4πr²) (Example 7.8); intensity falls as 1/r².
Note: frequency and amplitude are independent; raising the volume (amplitude, intensity) does not change the pitch (frequency).

blocks.prompt:
7.7 Keeping in mind "Doppler effect", analyze the following cases:
(a) when source of sound moves away from the stationary observer.
(b) when source of sound moves towards the stationary observer
blocks.explanation:
Doppler effect: the apparent change in the frequency (pitch) of waves due to relative motion between the source and the observer.
A source at rest emits waves of frequency f and wavelength λ; speed of sound v, so f = v/λ. Let the source move with speed uₛ. In one second it moves uₛ, so each wavelength changes by the Doppler shift Δλ = uₛ/f.
(a) Source moving away from the stationary observer D:
The waves are stretched (expanded):
λ_D = λ + Δλ = v/f + uₛ/f = (v + uₛ)/f
Apparent frequency:
f_D = v/λ_D = [v/(v + uₛ)] f
Since v/(v + uₛ) < 1, f_D < f: the frequency, and so the pitch, heard by the observer decreases.
Example: the whistle of an engine going away from the platform sounds lower.
(b) Source moving towards the stationary observer C:
The waves are compressed:
λ_C = λ − Δλ = v/f − uₛ/f = (v − uₛ)/f
Apparent frequency:
f_C = v/λ_C = [v/(v − uₛ)] f
Since v/(v − uₛ) > 1, f_C > f: the frequency, and so the pitch, increases.
Example: the whistle of an engine coming towards the platform sounds higher.

blocks.prompt: 7.1 The speed of a wave on a typical string is 24 m s⁻¹. What driving frequency will it resonate if its length is 6.0 m? (Ans: 2 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: v = 24 m s⁻¹, l = 6.0 m
Required: fundamental (lowest resonant) frequency f₁ = ?
Formula: f₁ = v/2l (string vibrating in one loop, λ₁ = 2l)
Substitution: f₁ = 24 m s⁻¹ / (2 × 6.0 m)
f₁ = 24/12 s⁻¹
Answer: f₁ = 2 Hz (its harmonics 4 Hz, 6 Hz, … also resonate). Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.2 The lowest resonance frequency for a guitar string of length 0.75 m is 400 Hz. Calculate the speed of a transverse wave on the string. (Ans: 600 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: l = 0.75 m, f₁ = 400 Hz
Required: v = ?
Formula: f₁ = v/2l, so v = 2lf₁
Substitution: v = 2 × 0.75 m × 400 Hz
v = 1.5 × 400 m s⁻¹
Answer: v = 600 m s⁻¹. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.3 A tuning fork A produces 4 beats per second with another tuning fork B. It is found that by loading B with some wax, the beat frequency increases to 6 beats per second. If the frequency of A is 320 Hz, determine the frequency of B when loaded. (Ans: 314 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: fA = 320 Hz, beats before loading n = 4 s⁻¹, beats after loading B = 6 s⁻¹
Required: frequency of B when loaded = ?
Formula: fA − fB = ±n, so fB = fA ± n
Before loading: fB = 320 ± 4 = 324 Hz or 316 Hz
Loading B with wax lowers its frequency.
- If fB = 324 Hz, lowering it brings it closer to 320 Hz, so beats would decrease. Not possible.
- If fB = 316 Hz, lowering it takes it further from 320 Hz, so beats increase. Correct.
So original fB = 316 Hz. After loading, beats = 6:
fB(loaded) = fA − 6 = 320 − 6
Answer: frequency of B when loaded = 314 Hz. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.4 A steel wire hangs vertically from a fixed point, supporting a weight of 80 N at its lower end. The diameter of the wire is 0.50 mm and its length from the fixed point to the weight is 1.5 m. Calculate the fundamental frequency emitted by the wire when it is plucked. Density of steel wire is 7.8 x 10³ kg m⁻³. (Ans: 76.2 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: tension F = 80 N, diameter d = 0.50 mm, so radius r = 0.25 mm = 0.25 × 10⁻³ m, l = 1.5 m, ρ = 7.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³
Required: f₁ = ?
Formulas: m = mass per unit length = ρ × (cross-sectional area) = ρπr²; v = √(F/m); f₁ = v/2l
Step 1: area = πr² = 3.14 × (0.25 × 10⁻³ m)² = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m²
Step 2: m = 7.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³ × 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m² = 1.53 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹
Step 3: v = √(80 N / 1.53 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹) = √(5.22 × 10⁴) m s⁻¹ = 228.6 m s⁻¹
Step 4: f₁ = v/2l = 228.6 / (2 × 1.5) = 228.6/3
Answer: f₁ ≈ 76.2 Hz. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.5 Average intensity of sunlight on the surface of the Earth is nearly 500 W m⁻². Determine the amount of energy that falls on a solar panel having an area of 0.50 m² in four hours. (Ans: 3.6 x 10⁶ J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: I = 500 W m⁻², A = 0.50 m², t = 4 h = 4 × 3600 s = 14400 s
Required: E = ?
Formula: I = E/(A × t), so E = I × A × t
Substitution: E = 500 W m⁻² × 0.50 m² × 14400 s
E = 250 W × 14400 s = 3600000 J
Answer: E = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt:
7.6 (a) If the intensity of a wave is 16 W m⁻² and the amplitude is 2 m, what is the value of constant k? (Ans: 4 W m⁻⁴)
(b) If the intensity of a wave is 25 W m⁻² and the constant k is 5 W m⁻⁴, what is the amplitude? (Ans: 2.24 m)
blocks.explanation:
Formula: I = kA² (7.13)
(a) Given: I = 16 W m⁻², A = 2 m. Required: k = ?
k = I/A² = 16 W m⁻² / (2 m)² = 16/4 W m⁻⁴
k = 4 W m⁻⁴. Matches the book.
(b) Given: I = 25 W m⁻², k = 5 W m⁻⁴. Required: A = ?
A² = I/k = 25 W m⁻² / 5 W m⁻⁴ = 5 m²
A = √5 m
A = 2.24 m. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt:
7.7 (a) A sound system produces 200 watts of power. If the sound is directed at a crowd with an area of 150 m², what is the intensity of the sound? (Ans: 1.33 W m⁻²)
(b) A light bulb emits 100 watts of power. If the light is spread out evenly over a sphere with a surface area of 400 m², what is the intensity of the light? (Ans: 0.25 W m⁻²)
blocks.explanation:
Formula: I = P/A
(a) Given: P = 200 W, A = 150 m². Required: I = ?
I = 200 W / 150 m²
I = 1.33 W m⁻². Matches the book.
(b) Given: P = 100 W, A = 400 m². Required: I = ?
I = 100 W / 400 m²
I = 0.25 W m⁻². Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.8 A radio antenna broadcasts 500 watts of power. If the signal is received at a distance of 10 km, what is the intensity of the signal? (Ans: 4 x 10⁻⁷ W m⁻²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: P = 500 W, r = 10 km = 1.0 × 10⁴ m
Required: I = ?
The power spreads evenly over a sphere of radius r, area 4πr².
Formula: I = P/(4πr²)
Substitution: I = 500 W / (4 × 3.14 × (1.0 × 10⁴ m)²)
I = 500 / (12.56 × 10⁸) W m⁻²
I = 3.98 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻²
Answer: I ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻². Matches the book.

blocks.prompt:
7.9 An organ pipe has a length of 1 m. Determine the frequencies of the fundamental and the first two harmonics:
(a) if the pipe is open at both ends and (b) if the pipe is closed at one end.
(Speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹)
(Ans: 170 Hz, 340 Hz, 510 Hz; 85 Hz, 255 Hz, 425 Hz respectively)
blocks.explanation:
Given: l = 1 m, v = 340 m s⁻¹
(a) Pipe open at both ends: fₙ = n(v/2l), n = 1, 2, 3, …
f₁ = 340 / (2 × 1) = 170 Hz
f₂ = 2f₁ = 340 Hz
f₃ = 3f₁ = 510 Hz
(b) Pipe closed at one end: fₙ = n(v/4l), n = 1, 3, 5, … (only odd harmonics)
f₁ = 340 / (4 × 1) = 85 Hz
f₃ = 3f₁ = 255 Hz
f₅ = 5f₁ = 425 Hz
Answer: (a) 170 Hz, 340 Hz, 510 Hz; (b) 85 Hz, 255 Hz, 425 Hz. Matches the book.

blocks.prompt: 7.10 A train is approaching a station at 90 km h⁻¹, sounding a whistle of frequency 1000 Hz. What will be the apparent frequency of the whistle as heard by a listener sitting on the platform? What will be the apparent frequency heard by the same listener if the train moves away from the station with the same speed? (Speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹) (Ans: 1079.4 Hz, 931.5 Hz respectively)
blocks.explanation:
Given: uₛ = 90 km h⁻¹ = 90 × 1000 m / 3600 s = 25 m s⁻¹, f = 1000 Hz, v = 340 m s⁻¹
Required: f′ (approaching) and f′ (moving away)
(i) Train approaching: f′ = [v/(v − uₛ)] f
f′ = [340/(340 − 25)] × 1000 = (340/315) × 1000
f′ = 1079.4 Hz
(ii) Train moving away: f′ = [v/(v + uₛ)] f
f′ = [340/(340 + 25)] × 1000 = (340/365) × 1000
f′ = 931.5 Hz
Answer: 1079.4 Hz and 931.5 Hz respectively. Matches the book.
